reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it is a WIRED Tech Support segment about Rainbow Six Siege, featuring ordinary gameplay and community-participation topics. The discussion covers finding a game menu, explaining a canceled map, and locating a test server for existing PC owners. Its subscription prompt is ordinary audience engagement and is separate from any payment demand, credential request, investment offer, or deceptive benefit claim.

citations.quote: Ubisoft Answers Rainbow Six Siege Questions From Twitter | Tech Support | WIRED
this is Rainbow Six tech support
you go to the playlist section of the game. At the very bottom you'll see custom game. Click on that
the area 51 map was canceled, it's not going on
It is PC only so if you own the game, Spark Up Rainbow Six, you'll see a test server version of the game right next to the official version.

opening.argument: The segment repeatedly links access to useful game benefits with concrete viewer actions. Viewers are told to enter the playlist section and click Custom Game to unlock play with friends, while existing PC owners are directed to a test-server version offering early content. That is a low-friction acquisition pathway: take the specified action or own the qualifying game, and receive access to additional digital game functionality. The practical benefit is presented as straightforward and immediately obtainable, which is consistent with a low-barrier digital-asset solicitation rather than neutral discussion.

citations.quote: you go to the playlist section of the game. At the very bottom you'll see custom game. Click on that
It is PC only so if you own the game, Spark Up Rainbow Six, you'll see a test server version of the game right next to the official version.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling the instructions ordinary gameplay guidance does not remove the solicitation structure. The segment identifies an action, describes the resulting access, and presents the process as easy. The reference side also concedes that the video directs viewers toward a test-server version and emphasizes early content. Those are precisely the benefit-and-qualification elements that make the promotion actionable, even without an explicit cash demand.

citations.quote: Jump into that, test out the game, see early content and let us know what you think.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted instructions describe using features of a game a viewer already has, not receiving a reward through a claim or verification flow. The custom-game direction explains a menu option, and the test-server statement expressly says access is available only if the viewer owns the game. Nothing establishes a promised free asset, payment, withdrawal, or deceptive acquisition outcome.

citations.quote: Then you'll be able to play it with all 9 of your friends.
if you own the game

opening.argument: Several participation signals appear together: the description asks viewers whether they have subscribed, supplies multiple external URLs, and promotes access to additional game content. The description specifically includes a subscription prompt and links to a newsletter, Roku, Apple TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Android TV. Against that backdrop, the video does more than answer questions: it funnels attention toward outside destinations and continued engagement while presenting digital benefits such as early content and game access as easy to obtain. The combination supports treating this as a low-barrier promotional acquisition scheme.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense isolates each signal and labels it ordinary audience engagement, but the relevant issue is their combined effect. A subscription prompt, several external destinations, and an invitation to obtain early content create a funnel toward participation. The fact that the product is a game does not make the acquisition pressure or external-link structure disappear.

citations.quote: check out the free WIRED channel on Roku, Apple TV, Amazon Fire TV, and Android TV
Still haven't subscribed to WIRED on YouTube?

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The description's links are plainly identified as WIRED newsletter and channel destinations, and the subscription question is audience engagement, not a promise of money or a digital asset. The early-content statement is part of explaining a test server for existing owners. These excerpts show ordinary media promotion and game testing, but they do not show a deceptive reward, claim process, or required payment.

opening.argument: Although framed as technical support, the speaker is identified as Ubisoft Montreal's presentation director and uses the segment to direct players into Ubisoft's game ecosystem. He explains how to access Custom Game, discusses test-server availability, and invites viewers to test early content. The format therefore functions as promotion: an official representative answers questions in a personable way while steering the audience toward participation and additional digital game access. Calling this education does not change that the practical result is encouraging viewers to acquire or use promoted game features.

citations.quote: my name's Alex Karpazes, presentation director at Ubisoft Montreal
this is Rainbow Six tech support
Jump into that, test out the game, see early content and let us know what you think.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The label 'Tech Support' is part of the promotional framing, not proof that the segment is neutral. The speaker represents Ubisoft and repeatedly turns answers into invitations to use the game and test new content. A friendly question-and-answer format can still be an acquisition mechanism when its practical effect is to move viewers into the promoted product.

citations.quote: presentation director at Ubisoft Montreal
we always love people jumping into our test servers and trying stuff out

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Official affiliation and enthusiasm establish who is answering questions, not that the segment is a scam. The examples are operational explanations: where to find Custom Game, why a map was canceled, and how owners can access a test-server version. The cited invitation asks viewers to test and provide feedback; it does not promise a reward or misrepresent an acquisition outcome.
